zufft

zufft computes fast Fourier, cosine and sine transforms in R. It bundles the BSD-licensed FFT code of ducc0, the same files and commit that SciPy uses, so it needs no system FFTW library and carries no GPL code.

  • Replaces fftwtools without FFTW. install.packages() is enough, on every platform, and the licence is MIT.
  • Fast. With CRAN’s build, faster than fftwtools on 30 of 33 benchmark cases and within 1.26 times on the rest; threads help further.
  • Familiar. Names a fftwtools user knows (fft_c2c(), fft_r2c(), fft_c2r()), the conventions of scipy.fft for axes, normalisation and cosine and sine transforms, and drop-in replacements for stats::fft() and stats::mvfft().

Installation

Install zufft from CRAN with:

install.packages("zufft")

or the development version from GitHub with:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zufft")

Example 

library(zufft)

x <- c(1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7)
fft_c2c(x)                       # full complex spectrum, as stats::fft(x)
#> [1]  27+0.000000e+00i  -5+5.196152e+00i   0+4.440892e-16i -11+0.000000e+00i
#> [5]   0-4.440892e-16i  -5-5.196152e+00i
X <- fft_r2c(x)                  # the non-redundant half
fft_c2r(X, n = length(x))        # and back
#> [1] 1 4 2 8 5 7

# columns of a matrix, on two threads
m <- matrix(rnorm(4096 * 64), 4096)
spec <- fft_r2c(m, axes = 1, workers = 2)
dim(spec)
#> [1] 2049   64

# cosine and sine transforms, SciPy's definitions
fft_dct(x, norm = "ortho")
#> [1] 11.0227038 -4.6508890 -1.0000000  0.4082483  0.0000000 -3.8343924
fft_dct(fft_dct(x), inverse = TRUE)
#> [1] 1 4 2 8 5 7

# fast lengths for zero-padding
fft_next_len(1009)
#> [1] 1024

Coming from fftwtools or scipy.fft

vignette("migrating-from-fftwtools") maps every fftwtools function to zufft. The one thing to remember is that zufft scales inverses by 1/n, as SciPy does; add norm = "none" for fftwtools’ (and stats::fft()’s) unscaled numbers. The scipy.fft article covers the Python side: the definitions match, and the test suite checks 2040 cases against SciPy.

Speed

zufft does not need a native build to keep up with fftwtools. On a Linux x86-64 runner, against fftwtools on Ubuntu’s FFTW (built with SSE2 and AVX vector code), one thread, from bench/RESULTS.md:

Case fftwtools zufft, CRAN build ratio zufft native, ratio
1-D complex 1 048 576 27.02 ms 20.64 ms 0.76 0.59
1-D real 1 000 000 16.50 ms 11.77 ms 0.71 0.57
columns real 1024 × 1024 5.97 ms 2.55 ms 0.43 0.34
2-D complex 2048² 279.85 ms 67.76 ms 0.24 0.19
3-D complex 128³ 44.80 ms 34.10 ms 0.76 0.83
1-D complex 100 000 1.44 ms 1.81 ms 1.26 0.83

A ratio below 1 means zufft is faster. With CRAN’s portable build (SSE2), zufft is faster on 30 of the 33 benchmark cases. The three where it is slower are single 1-D complex transforms of about 10^5 to 10^6 points that cannot be split into lines (worst 1.26 times). Built for the local CPU (below, AVX2 here), zufft is faster on all 33. Each ratio compares runs on the same machine; the two builds ran on separate runners.

Most of the margin comes from planning: zufft caches its plans, while fftwtools builds a new FFTW plan on every call. Threads add more (workers = 2), which fftwtools does not offer. Transforms of any length run in O(n log n): a prime length of 100 003 takes milliseconds, against seconds for stats::fft().

On Apple silicon the gap is wider, but partly because Homebrew’s FFTW has no vector code for double precision there; bench/RESULTS.md has those numbers too.

R stores arrays column by column, so the first dimension is the contiguous one. With axes = NULL the real transforms halve that dimension, which is fast and matches fftwtools; give axes explicitly to halve the last one listed, as SciPy does. Results are bit-identical whatever the number of threads.

Native build

CRAN’s binaries are compiled for any CPU of their architecture, so on x86-64 they use SSE2, two doubles per vector. On a CPU with AVX2 or AVX-512 a build for your own machine runs faster. Set ZUFFT_CXXFLAGS before installing from source; zufft adds it to its compiler flags and nothing else:

Sys.setenv(ZUFFT_CXXFLAGS = "-march=native")
install.packages("zufft", type = "source")
# or the development version: pak::pak("pedrobtz/zufft")

zufft::zufft_info()$simd_width   # 4 with AVX2, 8 with AVX-512; 2 is portable

This works on Linux and macOS; installing from source needs a compiler (on macOS, the Xcode command line tools). Windows builds ignore ZUFFT_CXXFLAGS and stay portable: code built for AVX by the GCC in Rtools crashed in our tests. On the Linux x86-64 runner of bench/RESULTS.md, where this gives AVX2, the 16384 × 64 complex column case drops from 15.39 ms to 9.17 ms and a complex prime length of 10 007 from 659.6 µs to 389.5 µs. On Apple silicon the vector width stays at two doubles, so a native build (-mcpu=native there) gains little.

Two things to know:

  • The package then runs only on CPUs like yours: do not copy the installed library to other machines.
  • With GCC on a CPU with fused multiply-add, results can differ in the last bit between thread counts; zufft::zufft_info()$fp_contract reports "fast" when that applies. CRAN’s builds report "off".

Licence

zufft is MIT-licensed. Its bundled ducc0 files are the “BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0-or-later” subset that SciPy vendors, used under BSD-3-Clause; inst/COPYRIGHTS lists every copyright holder. No GPL-only ducc0 code is included.
